title: Public Choice Theory
description: Buchanan and Tullock — politicians as self-interested agents

concepts.title: Applying Economics to Politics
concepts.contentHtml:
Standard economics models markets where self-interested agents pursue their own goals subject to constraints. Public choice theory applies the same lens to political behavior.

The radical move: treat politicians, voters, bureaucrats, and lobbyists as self-interested agents — not as benevolent stewards of the public good.

James Buchanan (Nobel 1986) and Gordon Tullock launched the modern field with The Calculus of Consent (1962). The term 'public choice' was Buchanan's.

The framework had immediate political implications. If government is run by self-interested agents, it doesn't automatically correct market failures — it has its own failures, with mechanisms that need analysis.

concepts.title: Voters as Rational Actors
concepts.contentHtml:
One striking implication: rational ignorance.

Voters' individual influence on election outcomes is microscopic. The expected benefit of being well-informed is tiny. The cost of becoming informed (time, attention) is real.

Anthony Downs argued: it's rational for voters to remain largely uninformed about policy. Most voters know little about most policy questions because the cost of learning exceeds expected return.

This isn't about voter stupidity — it's about incentive structure. Even smart voters face the calculation.

Implications: democratic outcomes don't aggregate detailed policy preferences. They aggregate broad signals, identity, partisanship, and attention-getting issues. Detailed policy is shaped by other actors — interest groups, bureaucracies, lobbyists.

Empirical evidence supports rational ignorance: polls consistently show voters know little about policy details, candidate positions on specific issues, or policy outcomes.

concepts.title: Concentrated Benefits, Diffuse Costs
concepts.contentHtml:
The single most important public-choice insight: policies often have concentrated benefits and diffuse costs.

A subsidy for sugar producers benefits a small group substantially. The cost — slightly higher sugar prices — falls on hundreds of millions of consumers, each barely noticing.

The political asymmetry: concentrated beneficiaries lobby intensely. Diffuse losers don't organize at all.

Result: policies favoring concentrated interests pass, even when their net welfare effect is negative. This explains:

– Persistent agricultural subsidies in rich countries.

– Trade protections for specific industries.

– Tax loopholes for narrow sectors.

– Occupational licensing.

– Regulations that protect incumbents from competition.

The pattern is structural — not corruption per se, but the natural equilibrium of self-interested political action. Reformers face an uphill battle: they need to organize the diffuse cost-bearers.

concepts.title: Politicians as Vote Maximizers
concepts.contentHtml:
If politicians want re-election, they pursue policies that maximize votes — not policies that maximize welfare.

The two diverge when:

– Beneficiaries are more politically active than cost-bearers (concentrated benefits, diffuse costs).

– Short-term effects differ from long-term ones (politicians prefer policies with visible short-term gains and deferred costs).

– Information is asymmetric (voters can't easily evaluate complex tradeoffs).

– Symbolic positions move voters more than actual policy effects.

This isn't moral failure — it's responsiveness to incentives. Politicians who don't pursue votes get replaced by ones who do.

Implications for institutional design: rules and constraints that limit political short-termism (independent central banks, balanced-budget rules, judicial review) can improve outcomes despite restricting democratic flexibility.

concepts.title: Strengths and Critiques
concepts.contentHtml:
Public choice has been highly influential. It explains many real political patterns — the persistence of inefficient policies, the asymmetric power of organized interests, the durability of democratic dysfunction.

Critiques:

Too cynical. Politicians and bureaucrats often do pursue public interest, not just self-interest. Treating them all as self-serving misses important behavioral motivations.

Politically loaded. Public choice has been used disproportionately to argue for smaller government. The framework's libertarian implications may exceed what the underlying analysis supports.

Underestimates ideology. Many policy debates are about values, not just incentives. Reducing political behavior to material self-interest misses what's actually being argued.

Mistakes individual rationality for collective. Even when voters are rational individually, collective decisions can be more or less rational than the average.

The synthesis: public choice insights are real and important. But they're descriptive, not prescriptive. Knowing that interest groups capture regulators doesn't mean having no regulators is better.

title: Voting & Arrow's Theorem
description: Why no perfect voting rule exists — Condorcet, Borda, Arrow's impossibility

concepts.title: Voting Rules
concepts.contentHtml:
How do you aggregate individual preferences into a collective decision?

Several voting rules:

Plurality (first-past-the-post): the candidate with the most first-place votes wins. Used in US, UK, India, many others.

Majority runoff: if no one gets a majority, top two compete in runoff. Used in France, many Latin American countries.

Borda count: voters rank candidates; rankings translate to points. Used in some non-political contests.

Approval voting: voters approve all acceptable candidates; the most-approved wins.

Ranked-choice (instant runoff): voters rank; candidates with fewest first-place votes are eliminated and votes redistributed. Used in Australia, parts of US.

Each rule produces different outcomes for the same preferences.

concepts.title: The Condorcet Paradox
concepts.contentHtml:
Marquis de Condorcet (1785) noticed a strange thing about majority rule.

Imagine three voters with these rankings of candidates A, B, C:

Voter 1: A > B > C

Voter 2: B > C > A

Voter 3: C > A > B

Now run head-to-head majority votes:

– A vs B: voters 1 and 3 prefer A; A wins 2-1.

– B vs C: voters 1 and 2 prefer B; B wins 2-1.

– C vs A: voters 2 and 3 prefer C; C wins 2-1.

So A beats B beats C beats A. Majority rule produces a cycle — no consistent winner.

This is the Condorcet paradox. Even with perfectly rational individual preferences, collective decisions can be intransitive.

concepts.title: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Kenneth Arrow (1951, Nobel 1972) generalized Condorcet's paradox into a sweeping impossibility result.

Define minimal conditions a 'good' voting rule should satisfy:

Universal domain: works for any preferences.

Pareto: if everyone prefers A to B, society does too.

Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives (IIA): social ranking of A vs B depends only on individual rankings of A vs B, not on other alternatives.

Non-dictatorship: no single voter decides outcomes.

Transitivity: social preferences are well-ordered (no cycles).

Arrow's Theorem: with three or more alternatives, no voting rule can satisfy all five conditions simultaneously.

This is striking. Democratic preference aggregation, on minimal axiomatic foundations, is provably impossible.

concepts.title: Which Axiom Is Worth Sacrificing?
concepts.contentHtml:
Different voting rules sacrifice different axioms. The choice reveals what we value.

Plurality voting can violate IIA (a 'spoiler' candidate changes the outcome) and Condorcet consistency (a candidate beaten head-to-head by all others can win).

Borda count violates IIA more dramatically. Adding alternatives can change rankings.

Approval voting isn't actually a preference-aggregation rule in the strict Arrow sense; it sidesteps some issues by asking different questions.

Ranked-choice can violate monotonicity (helping a candidate by ranking them higher can paradoxically hurt them).

No system is uniformly best. Each trades off Arrow's axioms differently. The choice depends on which violations matter most in context.

This is one reason voting reform debates are persistent and contentious — there's no neutrally 'best' system to settle on.

concepts.title: Beyond Arrow
concepts.contentHtml:
Arrow's theorem is a foundational impossibility, but it doesn't mean democracy is impossible.

Restrictions on preferences can rescue rules. If preferences are 'single-peaked' along a single dimension (a left-right spectrum), the median voter rule produces consistent outcomes (Black's median voter theorem).

Approximate rules can come close to satisfying all axioms even though no rule satisfies them exactly.

And in practice, voting works. Most democracies muddle through. Cycles do appear occasionally but aren't pervasive. Real preference distributions are usually structured enough that voting produces sensible outcomes most of the time.

Arrow's lesson isn't that democracy fails. It's that perfect preference aggregation is impossible, so we should think carefully about which imperfections to accept. There's no neutral 'will of the people'; the aggregation method is itself a choice with consequences.

title: Median Voter Theorem
description: Why two-party systems converge to the center — and when they don't

concepts.title: The Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Duncan Black's median voter theorem (1948): when voters have single-peaked preferences along a single dimension, majority rule produces the median voter's preferred outcome.

Setting: voters' preferences over a policy variable (say, government spending) are 'single-peaked' — each voter has a most-preferred level and prefers options closer to it over options further away.

Result: in pairwise majority voting, the median voter's preferred policy beats all alternatives. The median voter is decisive.

This is one of the cleanest results in political economy. It explains why politicians often converge to the center, why moderate policies persist, and why political competition tends to focus on capturing median voters.

concepts.title: Hotelling's Beach
concepts.contentHtml:
Harold Hotelling (1929) gave a vivid analogy.

Imagine two ice cream vendors on a beach. Where should each set up to maximize their share of beachgoers?

If vendor A sets up at one end and vendor B at the other, each gets half the beach.

But B can do better by moving slightly toward A — gaining customers in the middle without losing those on B's end.

A then moves toward B for the same reason. The equilibrium: both vendors at the center of the beach, splitting customers exactly.

The political analog: two parties competing for votes on a single ideological dimension converge to the median voter's position. The 'left' and 'right' parties end up indistinguishable in the middle.

This is often used to explain periods of US political convergence, such as the mid-20th century, when neither party drifted far from the center on many economic issues.

concepts.title: When Parties Don't Converge
concepts.contentHtml:
Real politics shows substantial divergence. Why doesn't the median voter theorem dominate?

Several reasons:

Multidimensional preferences. The single-dimension assumption is restrictive. With multiple dimensions, no clear median exists, and other coalitions can form.

Primary elections. US parties select candidates through primaries dominated by partisan voters. The primary median is far from the general-election median, pushing candidates toward extremes.

Turnout effects. Mobilizing your base can matter more than persuading swing voters. This rewards extreme positions that activate the base.

Donor influence. Big donors have positions away from the median. Candidates who please donors win resources.

Strong partisan identity. Voters increasingly choose party first, policy second. Convergence to median policies doesn't help if voters won't cross party lines anyway.

The result: Hotelling-style convergence happens in some periods (the mid-20th-century US) but not others (US 2010s-20s show striking polarization). Institutional features and political context matter.

concepts.title: Multi-Party Systems
concepts.contentHtml:
The theorem assumes two-party competition. Multi-party systems work differently.

In proportional representation, parties don't need to win majorities — they share power based on vote share. This creates space for parties at various positions, including ideologically extreme ones.

Coalitions form post-election. The 'pivotal' party — whose support is needed to form a majority — gains disproportionate power, often more than its vote share suggests.

European multi-party systems show: more parties on the spectrum, smaller parties that wield outsized influence as coalition members, more direct expression of ideological diversity, and coalition governments whose stability varies widely.

The US two-party system aggressively pushes politics into binary choices. Multi-party systems allow more nuance but require post-election bargaining to govern.

Neither model is universally better. Each has tradeoffs in representation, stability, and policy continuity.

concepts.title: Median Voter and Real Policy
concepts.contentHtml:
Despite the limitations, the median voter theorem captures real political dynamics.

Long-run outcomes in democracies tend to track median preferences. Wildly unpopular policies don't survive. Politicians who lose touch with the median get punished electorally.

But the theorem's clean prediction (exact convergence) is rarely exactly observed. Real politics involves multidimensional preferences, primary effects, voter mobilization, and institutional friction.

The result is something more like 'gravitational pull toward the median' — a force that operates alongside other forces (ideological commitment, donor pressure, identity politics).

Recent democracies have shown the limits. The US and UK have seen significant policy moves away from the median voter — partly because of institutional features (primaries, gerrymandering, electoral college) that allow non-median outcomes.

The lesson: the median voter theorem is a useful baseline, but real politics requires understanding what pulls outcomes away from it. Both forces are real and worth studying.

title: Rent Seeking
description: Tullock — the dissipation of resources in pursuit of artificial rents

concepts.title: What Is Rent Seeking?
concepts.contentHtml:
Gordon Tullock's 1967 paper asked a question. Standard economic analysis showed that monopolies create deadweight loss — but only the small triangle between the demand curve and marginal cost.

Tullock noticed something missed: creating the monopoly takes effort. Lobbying, legal fees, political contributions, public relations campaigns — all these consume resources.

This extra cost is rent seeking — using resources to capture or defend artificial rents (monopoly profits, regulatory protection, government contracts).

From a social perspective, rent seeking is pure waste. The lobbyist's salary doesn't produce anything useful; it just transfers wealth from one group to another while burning resources in the process.

concepts.title: The Magnitude
concepts.contentHtml:
How large is rent seeking?

Tullock's stylized result: in equilibrium, rent-seekers spend up to the full value of the rent they're competing for. If a monopoly is worth $10 billion, lobbyists collectively spend up to $10 billion to win it.

This full dissipation result is extreme but instructive. It says the social cost of monopoly isn't just the deadweight loss triangle — it's potentially the entire monopoly profit, plus the deadweight loss.

Real-world rent seeking is hard to measure precisely. Estimates of US lobbying expenditure: over $4 billion per year directly, with much more spent on related activities (campaign donations, think tanks, media, regulatory compliance).

This understates total rent-seeking, since many rent-seeking activities aren't classified as lobbying — corporate restructuring for tax purposes, regulatory arbitrage, legal manipulation.

Total cost is hard to pin down but plausibly several percent of GDP in advanced economies.

concepts.title: Examples
concepts.contentHtml:
Rent seeking takes many forms:

Trade protection lobbying: US sugar industry spending to maintain quotas and tariffs that raise sugar prices for consumers.

Regulatory capture: regulated industries lobbying to weaken regulations or shape them favorably. The classic case is the US occupational licensing of nurses, lawyers, and many trades.

Tax loopholes: corporate spending on lobbyists who craft narrow tax provisions benefiting specific industries.

Government contracts: companies investing heavily in government relations to win contracts that competitors would deliver more cheaply.

Patent trolling: firms acquiring patents not to produce anything but to extract licensing fees from real producers.

Litigation: using legal processes to extract value rather than create it. Predatory shareholder lawsuits, frivolous patent claims.

Each consumes resources without creating output. The aggregate is substantial.

concepts.title: Why Rent Seeking Persists
concepts.contentHtml:
If rent seeking is socially wasteful, why does it persist?

Because it's privately profitable. Each rent-seeker earns more than they spend. The waste is concentrated in the dissipation across all competitors plus the distortions caused by the rents themselves.

Other reasons:

– Path dependence: once an industry has captured a rent, dismantling it imposes immediate costs on workers and investors. Political capital is needed to remove rents.

– Information asymmetry: rents are often disguised as something else (consumer protection, infant industry, national security).

– Coalition logic: rents create coalitions of beneficiaries with concentrated incentives to preserve them. Diffuse cost-bearers don't organize.

– Reform is risky: politicians who challenge rent-seeking face well-funded opposition.

Reducing rent seeking requires structural changes — campaign finance reform, lobbying transparency, streamlined regulation, judicial limits on regulatory creation. Many advanced economies have made progress; few have eliminated rent seeking.

concepts.title: Implications for Development
concepts.contentHtml:
Rent seeking has special importance for poor countries.

In countries with weak institutions, large rents are available — natural resource revenues, regulatory monopolies, government contracts. The expected gain from successful rent seeking can exceed gains from productive activity.

Result: talented people pursue rent seeking instead of innovation, entrepreneurship, or genuine value creation. The aggregate effect is to slow growth substantially.

Murphy, Shleifer, and Vishny (1991) modeled this formally. When rents are large, the economy can be stuck in a low-equilibrium where the most talented engage in rent seeking. Reducing rents reorients talent toward production and accelerates growth.

This connects to the resource curse — countries with abundant natural resources often grow more slowly than resource-poor ones. The mechanism is partly through enhanced rent-seeking opportunities.

Implications for development policy: institutional reforms that limit rent seeking (clear property rights, regulatory simplification, judicial independence) are growth-promoting beyond their direct effects. The intermediate target — making rent seeking less profitable than production — is the deeper goal.

title: Institutions & Property Rights
description: North, Coase — transaction costs, contract enforcement, the state as guarantor

concepts.title: North on Institutions
concepts.contentHtml:
Douglass North (Nobel 1993) defined institutions as 'the rules of the game in a society' — both formal (laws, constitutions, contracts) and informal (norms, conventions).

His argument: institutions structure incentives. Bad institutions reward unproductive behavior; good institutions reward productive behavior.

Why do some societies have good institutions and others don't? North traced the evolution of institutions through history — from feudalism to capitalism, from local trade networks to global markets.

Institutional development is path-dependent: early choices about property rights, political authority, and contract enforcement create feedback loops that lock in particular trajectories. Britain's Glorious Revolution of 1688 set institutional patterns that lasted centuries.

Modern economic prosperity rests on a particular institutional configuration that took centuries to develop. It's not the natural state; it's a hard-won achievement.

concepts.title: Property Rights
concepts.contentHtml:
Without secure property rights, productive investment doesn't pay. Why grow crops if soldiers will take them? Why build a factory if the state may seize it?

Property rights have three dimensions:

Ownership clarity: who owns what?

Use rights: what can the owner do with their property?

Transfer rights: can the owner sell, lease, or bequeath?

Each dimension matters separately. A peasant might 'own' land but not be allowed to sell it (Soviet collective farms). A firm might own assets but face arbitrary expropriation (resource-curse states). A landlord might own buildings but be unable to evict tenants (rent control).

Effective property rights require legal infrastructure: courts, registry systems, enforcement mechanisms. They also require political stability — knowing the rights won't be undermined by the next government.

Hernando de Soto's work showed how weak property rights in poor countries trap wealth. Slum residents have homes but no legal title; their property can't serve as collateral for loans or be reliably transferred. Formal property rights would unlock trillions of dollars of dead capital.

concepts.title: Coase and Transaction Costs
concepts.contentHtml:
Ronald Coase (Nobel 1991) showed that transaction costs shape economic organization.

His The Nature of the Firm (1937): why do firms exist at all? Because organizing activity within a firm has different transaction costs than organizing it through markets. Firms exist where internal coordination is cheaper than market exchange.

His Problem of Social Cost (1960): externalities can be solved through bargaining if transaction costs are zero — but real bargaining costs are positive, often prohibitive. Property rights and legal rules matter precisely because bargaining is costly.

The framework reframed economics. Markets aren't 'natural' — they require institutional infrastructure to function. The choice between market organization, firms, and government provision depends on which has lower transaction costs in the specific context.

Modern applications: digital platforms reducing transaction costs (Uber, Airbnb), supply chain organization, the make-or-buy decision, regulation of contracts. All build on Coase's framework.

concepts.title: Contract Enforcement
concepts.contentHtml:
Markets require enforceable contracts. Without enforcement, parties can break deals freely; risk-bearing collapses; long-term commitments become impossible.

Sources of enforcement:

Courts and law: the formal mechanism. Effective in countries with rule of law and judicial independence.

Reputation: repeated interaction creates incentive to honor commitments. Trade networks, business communities.

Social pressure: norms and shame can enforce contracts in tight communities.

Self-enforcing contracts: design contracts so that breach is unprofitable.

Private enforcement: arbitration, escrow services, credit reporting.

The state's role is foundational. Even where reputation suffices for many deals, large or unusual transactions need legal backstop.

Countries with weak court systems suffer profound economic costs. Loans require excessive collateral; markets stay informal; firms remain small (only family members can be trusted with significant resources). The cost of weak enforcement falls heavily on growth.

concepts.title: Why Institutions Persist
concepts.contentHtml:
If good institutions are so valuable, why don't all countries copy them?

Several reasons.

Political resistance. Bad institutions often benefit specific elites. Reform threatens their power.

Coordination failure. Even when reform would help everyone in the long run, transitions are risky and slow. Investing in new institutions before they're trusted is hard.

Path dependence. Institutions are interconnected. You can't easily transplant courts without supporting cultures, legal traditions, and educational systems.

Tacit knowledge. Effective institutions rely on accumulated practices and norms that take generations to develop.

Acemoglu-Robinson elite blocking. Successful reform requires changing the political coalitions that benefit from existing institutions — not just changing rules on paper.

The implication: institutional reform is genuinely hard. External imposition (US-led nation building, World Bank conditionality) has rarely succeeded. Successful institutional development typically requires domestic reform coalitions, gradual changes, and patient sequencing.

This is humbling. We know reasonably well what good institutions look like. We don't know reliably how to create them. The gap is one of the deepest puzzles in development economics — and the central question of political economy.
